title: Raja Yoga)
hook: you can't see the bottom of a lake while the wind is blowing

segments.voice: Yesterday in Raja Yoga, the monkey: restless, drunk on desire, stung by jealousy, possessed by pride, and Vivekananda's first lesson, which was simply to watch the monkey jump. Did you catch a jump? Day nine hundred forty-eight.

Stand at the edge of a lake on a windy afternoon. The surface is all chop and glitter. Somewhere down there are stones, weeds, maybe a lost key, but you can't see any of it. Come back at dawn, when the air is still. The same water. Now you can count the pebbles. Nothing was added to the lake overnight. Something was taken away. Vivekananda uses that lake to explain one short line near the start of the Yoga Sutras.
screen: `A LAKE ON A WINDY DAY.` → `THE SAME LAKE AT DAWN.` → `NOTHING ADDED. SOMETHING STILLED.`

segments.voice: Raja Yoga carries, in its second half, Vivekananda's own rendering of the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, short lines with his explanation under each. Near the very start is the line that says what yoga is. Put plainly, it says yoga is the stilling of the waves of the mind. The Sanskrit word for the mind-stuff is chitta. The word for its waves, the shapes it keeps taking, is vritti. And Vivekananda reaches for a lake. The bottom of the lake, he says, is our own true self. The lake is the chitta, and the waves are the vrittis. While the surface is rippled, we can't see the bottom. If the water is muddy, we can't see it either. Only when the water is clear and the waves die down do we see what was there the whole time. Notice what that does to the goal. Nobody has to build a self, or earn one, or go and find one somewhere else. The claim in this picture is that it's already lying at the bottom, and the work is to let the surface settle. So yesterday's monkey and today's lake belong together. Watching the monkey is how you learn where the wind is coming from. Stilling the waves is what the watching is for. Vivekananda doesn't pretend it's quick. The waves keep rising: a craving, an insult remembered, a plan for tomorrow. Each one hides the bottom for a while. Each time one settles, the water is a little clearer. That's the yoga of the mind, as this book teaches it: not adding something to yourself, but letting the water clear.
screen: `YOGA STILLS THE WAVES OF THE MIND.` · `THE LAKE IS CHITTA. THE WAVES ARE VRITTIS.` · `THE BOTTOM IS THE TRUE SELF.` · then, large: `LET THE WATER CLEAR.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath slow on its own. Bring to mind a lake, any lake, under a little wind. Now, each time a thought rises, see it as a wave on that surface. Don't push the wave flat. Just let it be a wave, and watch it pass back into the water. Then the next one. Some will be big. Some will be small. Between them, for a moment, the surface may go still, and you may see a little further down. If you pray, you can rest in that stillness as your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Raja Yoga. Vivekananda's yoga of the mind, which he explains with a lake: still the waves, and the bottom, the true self, was there all along.
Your line: let the water clear. Today, when something stirs you up, before you answer, give the water one slow breath to settle and see what's under the wave. Day nine hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: People who follow Vivekananda's teaching read Patanjali's Yoga Sutras with his explanations and keep a daily sit aimed at quieting the mind; the Ramakrishna Mission and Vedanta Societies hold classes on the text.
